director.chapterArc: A journey from sensory disorientation to tactical clarity and finally to a quiet, ominous realization of supernatural threat.
director.restraintNote: Maintain Jab's exhausted practicality; do not dramatize the fear until the hounds are confirmed. The horror is in the stillness and the arithmetic of survival.

cues.delivery: Measured observation. Jab's distrust is internal and physical; the narrator should feel grounded in his sensory confusion.
cues.from: The road went down out of the snow at about the middle of the morning, and by noon there was no snow at all, and Jab found that he did not trust it.
cues.through: It was the same road. That was the strange part. It had the same raised bed and the same ditch either side and the same hard grey surface under his boots, and somewhere in the last two miles it had simply stopped being white. There was frost in the shadow of the ditch banks and ice standing in the wheel ruts of the field tracks, and the fields themselves were brown and bare and enormous, going away east to a river he could see in pieces. Behind him the hills had their winter on. Down here the country was only cold.
cues.reason: Establishes the uncanny feeling of a familiar road that has changed.

cues.delivery: Jab's voice is low and economical. Tonk's lines are breathy but factual; no whining.
cues.through: "I said today. It's today. I didn't say now."
cues.reason: Dialogue establishes the tension of time passing without panic.

cues.delivery: Clinical precision. Jab's realization about the smell is a medical assessment, not an emotional outburst.
cues.from: He knew why. He had known since he unwrapped the leg in the grey before dawn and the smell had come up at him and been different. Not worse in the way it had been getting worse for a week — different, the way milk is different.
cues.reason: The shift from 'worse' to 'different' requires clarity.

cues.delivery: Narrative pacing slows slightly as Jab processes the social isolation. The carter's dialogue is clipped and efficient.
cues.from: At the second hour there were people on the road.
cues.through: "Gate's open till dark," he said, over his shoulder, already past. "They'll not shut it early on you."
cues.reason: Contrast between Jab's internal panic and external stillness.

cues.delivery: Dry, observational. Tonk's comment on rudeness is a child's literal interpretation; Jab's laugh should be brief and tired.
cues.through: "Say hello to one," Tonk said, with the air of a man making a fair offer, and Jab, who had been dreading the next person on the road for the last quarter of an hour, laughed and found that he had stopped dreading them quite so much.
cues.reason: Brief levity to ground the scene before the exposition.

cues.delivery: Expository rhythm. The old man's advice is delivered with flat urgency; Jab repeats 'Clinical' as a mantra.
cues.from: It was a trick he had from the smoke house. When his father's aunt wanted to know something she never asked it. She said a thing she already knew, slightly wrong, and stood there while somebody corrected her, and by the end of the correcting she had the whole of it and had never once been a person who did not know.
cues.through: "Then say it twice," said the old man.
cues.reason: Critical information delivery must be clear and unadorned.

cues.delivery: Jab's internal monologue about 'flatness' is rhythmic and deliberate. Tonk's observation of the fish count breaks his focus.
cues.from: They stopped at the third hour in the lee of a stone sheep-fold twenty paces off the road, because Tonk had gone from talking to not talking in about a mile, and Jab had learned to stop at the change rather than at the bottom.
cues.through: Jab sat in the dry grass beside a stone wall with his brother's whole chest going up and down too fast under a hide, and laughed until his eyes ran, and then wiped his face with his sleeve before he turned round.
cues.reason: The shift from medical assessment to child interaction.

cues.delivery: Dialogue with the second carter. Jab's responses are short; the carter's warning about 'Hounds' is delivered as a matter of fact.
cues.from: The carter came up on them at the fourth hour, going the same way, and this one stopped.
cues.through: "Bad by tomorrow, or bad by next week?"
cues.reason: The threat must feel real but not melodramatic.

cues.delivery: Jab's internal arithmetic. The decision to reject the shed is a calculated risk; Jab speaks with finality.
cues.from: He went and stood at the wall for a while with his back to both of them.
cues.through: "It's a real sum," he said. "The other one's in there. I know it's in there. But if I sit in your shed tonight and he turns, I'll have the whole of the rest of my life to think about the mile."
cues.reason: The pivot point of the chapter: choosing immediate danger over delayed death.

cues.delivery: The carter's gift is given with a weary kindness. Jab accepts it without gratitude or drama.
cues.from: "Right," he said, and turned round and started untying one of his sacks, which was not what Jab had braced for at all. "Then you'll take this, and you'll not argue with me about it, because I've stood here and failed to talk you into a stove and I'm going to be allowed to do something."
cues.through: "Because I had a girl with a bad hip," he said, "and I've had the chair on this cart for nine years and I've never once got round to mending the arm of it." He clicked his tongue at the pony. "Go on, then. Go fast and don't stop in the sag, and if something stands still and looks at you, don't you stand still and look back."
cues.reason: Maintain the transactional nature of their interaction.

cues.delivery: Atmospheric shift. The road becomes treacherous; Jab's heart rate is implied through pacing.
cues.from: The last of the light went out of the sky at the fifth hour, and it went fast, the way it did in winter in a flat country, and Jab was still a mile and a half out.
cues.through: Jab stood still in the middle of the road with his heart going and did the thing he had promised himself for sixteen days that he would not do on this last stretch.
cues.reason: Building tension before the blade activation.

cues.delivery: The lighting of the blade is a tactile action. Jab's focus shifts to survival; Tonk's voice returns.
cues.through: Jab held it out a little to the side, where his brother could see the whole of it, and walked on down the middle of a straight road with an amber line burning on his fist and a boy watching it over his shoulder.
cues.reason: The visual shift from darkness to amber light.

cues.delivery: Jab's exhaustion is physical. The final line must land with a sense of impending dread.
cues.from: It cost him. He had known that too. Holding the shape was nothing after four years, but holding the light was a small steady drip out of a bucket that had almost nothing in it, and by the time he had gone four hundred paces he could feel the drip.
cues.through: And somewhere in the third verse, out in the ditch on the left, at the edge of what the amber line could show him, something that had been keeping station with him stopped.
cues.reason: The chapter ends on the realization that they are being watched.

pauses.after: The road went down out of the snow at about the middle of the morning, and by noon there was no snow at all, and Jab found that he did not trust it.
pauses.reason: Completed thought; Jab's distrust of the road needs a beat to settle.

pauses.reason: Completed thought; the instruction to say 'Clinical' needs weight.

pauses.after: "There's five," said Tonk, from the hide, without opening his eyes. "You counted them at the fire. You always say nothing and it's always the fish and there's five."
pauses.reason: Speaker reset. Jab's laugh breaks his internal tension before the carter arrives.

pauses.reason: Major emotional landing. The diagnosis of 'bad by tomorrow' is a critical plot turn.
